claim: Sox2 is detected on chromatin fractions from synchronized populations, including mitotic cells.
source: We detected Sox2 on chromatin fractions from synchronized populations, including mitotic cells (Figure 1A), providing initial evidence that Sox2 may associate with mitotic chromosomes.
evidence: Supported by biochemical fractionation data shown in Figure 1A

claim: TBP fractionates with mitotic chromosomes whereas Pol II does not.
source: Similarly, TBP fractionated with mitotic chromosomes whereas Pol II did not (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by biochemical fractionation data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2

claim: In asynchronous populations, the majority of Sox2 fractionates at high salt and in the micrococcal nuclease-digested chromatin, suggesting a strong interaction of Sox2 with chromatin.
source: In the asynchronous population, the majority of Sox2 fractionated at high salt and in the micrococcal nuclease-digested chromatin, suggesting a strong interaction of Sox2 with chromatin (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by salt fractionation data shown in Figure 1B and interpreted based on the principle that nuclear transcription factors elute at salt concentrations that overcome their binding strength to DNA

claim: Oct4 fractionates with much lower salt concentrations than Sox2.
source: In contrast, Oct4 fractionated with much lower salt concentrations (Figure 1B), consistent with its more dynamic association with chromatin (Chen et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by salt fractionation data shown in Figure 1B and consistent with published literature on Oct4 dynamics

claim: Sox2 displays a similar salt fractionation profile in synchronized mitotic cells as in asynchronous cells, albeit with a somewhat reduced signal in the digested chromatin.
source: Sox2 displayed a similar salt fractionation profile in synchronized mitotic cells, albeit with a somewhat reduced signal in the digested chromatin (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by salt fractionation data shown in Figure 1B

claim: Sox2 likely associates with mitotic chromosomes in a manner that is qualitatively weaker than its association with interphase chromatin.
source: Taken together with the biochemical fractionation assay, these data suggest that Sox2 likely associates with mitotic chromosomes in a manner that is qualitatively weaker than its association with interphase chromatin.
evidence: Inferred from biochemical fractionation and salt fractionation data showing reduced signal in mitotic chromatin

claim: Sox2 is largely excluded from mitotic chromosomes when analyzed by immunofluorescence in standard formaldehyde-fixed mouse ES cells.
source: In contrast to our biochemical data, we found that Sox2 is largely excluded from mitotic chromosomes (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1C

claim: Overexpressed Halo-tagged Sox2 is highly enriched on mitotic chromosomes when imaged under live-cell conditions.
source: However, when we over-expressed Halo-tagged Sox2 (Halo-Sox2 OE) in mouse ES cells stably expressing H2B-GFP and imaged mitotic cells under live-cell conditions, we observed that Halo-Sox2 is highly enriched on mitotic chromosomes (Figure 1D).
evidence: Supported by live-cell imaging data shown in Figure 1D

claim: Endogenously tagged Halo-Sox2 KI is highly enriched on mitotic chromosomes under live-cell conditions.
source: Imaging under live-cell conditions, we confirmed that Halo-Sox2 KI is indeed highly enriched on mitotic chromosomes (Figure 1D).
evidence: Supported by live-cell imaging data shown in Figure 1D

claim: Strong enrichment of Halo-Sox2 KI to chromosomes is detected throughout all stages of mitosis.
source: Furthermore, using time-lapse microscopy, we detected strong enrichment of Halo-Sox2 KI to chromosomes throughout all stages of mitosis (Figure 1E).
evidence: Supported by time-lapse microscopy data shown in Figure 1E

claim: Both the HaloTag and α-Sox2 signals in fixed cell preparations are excluded from mitotic chromosomes.
source: Surprisingly, both the HaloTag and the α-Sox2 signals in these fixed cell preparations were found to be excluded from mitotic chromosomes as marked by H2B-GFP (Figure 1F) in contrast to the live-cell imaging results.
evidence: Supported by fixed cell imaging data shown in Figure 1F

claim: Both Halo-Sox2 OE and Halo-Sox2 KI switch from positive enrichment under live-cell imaging conditions to exclusion after fixation.
source: With this metric, both Halo-Sox2 OE and Halo-Sox2 KI switched from positive enrichment under live-cell imaging conditions to exclusion after fixation (Figure 1H), suggesting that fixation by paraformaldehyde results in the exclusion of Sox2 from mitotic chromosomes.
evidence: Supported by quantitative analysis of chromosome enrichment shown in Figure 1H

claim: Formaldehyde may uniquely alter the structure of HMGB proteins and thus result in exclusion from mitotic chromosomes.
source: This result is reminiscent of a previous study showing that HMGB proteins become excluded from mitotic chromosomes after fixation (Pallier et al., 2003). The authors argue that formaldehyde may uniquely alter the structure of HMGB proteins and thus result in exclusion, which may be consistent with Sox2 as it contains an HMG domain.
evidence: Supported by citation to Pallier et al., 2003

claim: The level of enrichment on mitotic chromosomes dramatically decreases after fixation for all tested TFs including Oct4, Esrrb, Klf4, Sp1, Foxo1, Foxo3a, Stat3, and Hsf1.
source: In all cases, the level of enrichment on mitotic chromosomes dramatically decreased after fixation, resulting in an apparent exclusion of all TFs examined (Figure 1I and Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 1I and Figure 1—figure supplement 4

claim: When imaged under live-cell conditions, the majority of tested TFs exhibit varying levels on mitotic chromosomes, from highly enriched to uniform levels.
source: When imaged under live-cell conditions, however, the majority of these factors exhibited varying levels on mitotic chromosomes, from highly enriched to uniform levels.
evidence: Supported by live-cell imaging data shown in Figure 1I

claim: Stat3 and Hsf1 are excluded from mitotic chromosomes under live-cell conditions.
source: We found two TFs that are excluded from mitotic chromosomes under live-cell conditions, Stat3 and Hsf1 (Figure 1I), both of which are known to require external signals to translocate into the nucleus during interphase.
evidence: Supported by live-cell imaging data shown in Figure 1I and known biological properties of Stat3 and Hsf1

claim: A large number of TFs are associated with mitotic chromosomes in chicken DT40 cells.
source: This is consistent with a study showing a large number of TFs associated with mitotic chromosomes in chicken DT40 cells (Ohta et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ohta et al., 2010

claim: Chemical fixation evicts TFs from mitotic chromosomes.
source: We have also tested other commonly used fixation methods and have varied the fused tag, and all the results suggest that chemical fixation somehow evicts TFs from mitotic chromosomes (Figure 1—figure supplement 5).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5

claim: A large body of literature spanning several decades of studying TFs during mitosis may have been founded in large part on a fixation artifact.
source: This surprising finding suggests that a large body of literature spanning several decades of studying TFs during mitosis, from their widely accepted exclusion from mitotic chromosomes to the apparent uniqueness of certain select TFs as specialized 'mitotic bookmarkers', may have been founded in large part on a fixation artifact.
evidence: Inferred from the finding that chemical fixation causes TF exclusion from mitotic chromosomes

claim: The HMG domain of Sox2 is sufficient to render mitotic chromosome localization.
source: When we quantified the chromosome enrichment of the truncations, we observed that the HMG domain is sufficient to render mitotic chromosome localization (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by quantitative analysis of Sox2 truncations shown in Figure 2B

claim: Halo-Sox2 TAD is mostly cytoplasmic.
source: Halo-Sox2 HMG became highly enriched on mitotic chromosomes whereas Halo-Sox2 TAD was mostly cytoplasmic (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by live-cell imaging data shown in Figure 2B

claim: Mutations of DNA binding residues in Sox2 result in exclusion from mitotic chromosomes under live-cell imaging conditions.
source: Expressed in ES cells, mutations of DNA binding residues resulted in exclusion from mitotic chromosomes under live-cell imaging conditions (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by live-cell imaging data shown in Figure 2B

claim: DNA binding is necessary for mitotic enrichment of Sox2.
source: Expressing this construct (Halo-Sox2 DBD3M) also showed exclusion from mitotic chromosomes (Figure 2B), confirming that DNA binding is necessary for mitotic enrichment.
evidence: Supported by live-cell imaging data shown in Figure 2B

claim: Mutations to the NLS of Sox2 result in exclusion from mitotic chromosomes.
source: Surprisingly, mutations to the NLS also resulted in exclusion from mitotic chromosomes (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by live-cell imaging data shown in Figure 2B

claim: Mutants of HNF1B become enriched on mitotic chromosomes following cold shock, and this enrichment is dependent on nuclear import.
source: For instance, mutants of HNF1B become enriched on mitotic chromosomes following cold shock, and that this enrichment is dependent on nuclear import (Lerner et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lerner et al., 2016

claim: The SV-40 NLS enriches the HaloTag protein in mitotic chromosomes.
source: When imaged under live conditions, we discovered that the NLS enriched the HaloTag protein in mitotic chromosomes (Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by live-cell imaging data shown in Figure 2C

claim: HaloTag protein alone is excluded from mitotic chromosomes.
source: In contrast, HaloTag protein alone is excluded from mitotic chromosomes (Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by live-cell imaging data shown in Figure 2C

claim: Halo-Plant NLS shows no enrichment on mitotic chromosomes.
source: When imaged under live-cell conditions, we observed no enrichment of Halo-Plant NLS on mitotic chromosomes (Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by live-cell imaging data shown in Figure 2C

claim: Both sequence-specific binding and active nuclear import likely contribute to the enrichment of TFs on mitotic chromosomes.
source: These results suggest that both sequence-specific binding and active nuclear import likely contribute to the enrichment of TFs on mitotic chromosomes.
evidence: Inferred from experiments showing that DNA binding mutations and NLS mutations both result in exclusion, and that functional NLS is required for enrichment

claim: Halo-Sox2 recovery is faster in mitotic cells than during interphase.
source: Quantifying intensities at the bleach spot over time shows that Halo-Sox2 recovery is faster in mitotic cells than during interphase, but significantly slower than Halo-NLS (Figure 3B).
evidence: Supported by FRAP data shown in Figure 3B

claim: The average time for Halo-Sox2 to reach 90% recovery in interphase is 19.7 s, whereas 90% recovery in mitosis is 4.3 s on average.
source: The average time for Halo-Sox2 to reach 90% recovery in interphase is 19.7 s, whereas 90% recovery in mitosis is 4.3 s on average (Figure 3C).
evidence: Supported by FRAP data shown in Figure 3C

claim: Halo-NLS reaches 90% recovery in 0.9 s for both interphase and mitotic cells.
source: In contrast, Halo-NLS reaches 90% recovery in 0.9 s for both interphase and mitotic cells (Figure 3C).
evidence: Supported by FRAP data shown in Figure 3C

claim: The interaction of Sox2 with mitotic chromosomes is more dynamic than its interaction with interphase chromatin.
source: These results suggest that the interaction of Sox2 with mitotic chromosomes is more dynamic than its interaction with interphase chromatin.
evidence: Inferred from FRAP data showing faster recovery in mitosis

claim: The residence time of specific Halo-Sox2 binding events during mitosis is 54% relative to interphase.
source: After correction for photobleaching, the residence time of specific Halo-Sox2 binding events during mitosis is 54% relative to interphase (Figure 3D inset).
evidence: Supported by single particle tracking data shown in Figure 3D

claim: In interphase, 30.9% of Halo-Sox2 molecules are bound, whereas 18.3% of Halo-Sox2 molecules are bound in mitosis.
source: In interphase, 30.9% of Halo-Sox2 molecules are bound, whereas 18.3% of Halo-Sox2 molecules are bound in mitosis (Figure 3E inset), an almost two-fold decrease in bound population.
evidence: Supported by single particle tracking data shown in Figure 3E

claim: There are fewer Sox2 molecules bound during mitosis, and these bound molecules experience a faster off-rate in mitosis.
source: Taken together with the slow tracking SPT analysis, these data suggest that there are fewer Sox2 molecules bound during mitosis, and that these bound molecules experience a faster off-rate in mitosis.
evidence: Inferred from single particle tracking data showing decreased bound fraction and decreased residence time in mitosis

claim: Halo-Sox2 HMG shows faster FRAP recovery both in interphase and mitosis compared to full length Halo-Sox2.
source: Compared to full length Halo-Sox2, the Halo-Sox2 HMG showed faster FRAP recovery both in interphase and mitosis (Figure 3B–C).
evidence: Supported by FRAP data shown in Figure 3B-C

claim: The average time for Halo-Sox2 HMG to reach 90% recovery in both interphase and mitosis is 6.6 s.
source: Indeed, the average time for Halo-Sox2 HMG to reach 90% recovery in both interphase and mitosis is 6.6 s, comparable to Halo-Sox2 in mitosis (4.3 s) (Figure 3C).
evidence: Supported by FRAP data shown in Figure 3C

claim: The TAD plays a significant role in stabilizing Sox2 interactions with interphase chromatin.
source: These results suggest that the TAD plays a significant role in stabilizing Sox2 interactions with interphase chromatin.
evidence: Inferred from FRAP data showing that Sox2 HMG (lacking TAD) has faster recovery in interphase similar to full-length Sox2 in mitosis

claim: The TAD region participates in interactions with partner proteins, including Oct4 and p300, to activate transcription.
source: The TAD region participates in interactions with partner proteins, including Oct4 and p300, to activate transcription (Cox et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Cox et al., 2010

claim: During mitosis, transcription is shut off globally, and therefore, the full length Sox2 now interacts with mitotic chromosomes primarily through its DNA binding domain, rendering the TAD inactive.
source: During mitosis, transcription is shut off globally, and therefore, the full length Sox2 now interacts with mitotic chromosomes primarily through its DNA binding domain, rendering the TAD inactive.
evidence: Inferred from FRAP data and known biology of mitotic transcriptional shutdown

claim: The length distribution profile of sequenced fragments from asynchronous cell populations and synchronized mitotic cells revealed near super-imposable patterns in Tn5 integration.
source: The length distribution profile of sequenced fragments from asynchronous cell populations and synchronized mitotic cells revealed near super-imposable patterns in Tn5 integration (Figure 4A), including the 10 bp periodicity patterns that mark DNA helical pitch (Figure 4A inset).
evidence: Supported by ATAC-seq data shown in Figure 4A

claim: Tn5 transposase may access mitotic chromosomes as equally well as interphase chromatin.
source: These nearly identical integration patterns and sequencing read counts (Figure 4—figure supplement 1) suggest that Tn5 transposase may access mitotic chromosomes as equally well as interphase chromatin.
evidence: Inferred from ATAC-seq data showing similar integration patterns and read counts

claim: There is little qualitative difference in peak patterns and intensities between asynchronous and mitotic cells when analyzing both the short reads and the mono-nucleosome sized fragments.
source: Similar to the total mapped reads, there is little qualitative difference in peak patterns and intensities between asynchronous and mitotic cells when we analyze both the short reads and the mono-nucleosome sized fragments (Figure 4C).
evidence: Supported by ATAC-seq data shown in Figure 4C

claim: Linear regression analysis of peak intensities between asynchronous and mitotic cells shows the slope of the fit at 0.965, with an R2 value of 0.991.
source: Indeed, linear regression analysis shows the slope of the fit at 0.965, with an R2 value of 0.991 (Figure 4D).
evidence: Supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 4D

claim: Mitotic chromosomes are accessed by the Tn5 transposase in nearly the same manner as it accesses interphase chromatin.
source: These quantitative analyses indicate that mitotic chromosomes are accessed by the Tn5 transposase in nearly the same manner as it accesses interphase chromatin, suggesting that the massive condensation of mitotic chromosomes has little effect on DNA accessibility.
evidence: Inferred from ATAC-seq data showing similar integration patterns and intensities between asynchronous and mitotic cells

claim: The peak of ATAC-seq reads in between the two well-positioned nucleosomes at the Oct4 distal enhancer is maintained in mitosis.
source: Importantly, the peak of ATAC-seq reads in between the two well-positioned nucleosomes is maintained in mitosis (Figure 5A).
evidence: Supported by ATAC-seq data shown in Figure 5A

claim: Mitosis integration density at Sox2 bound sites is roughly 60% of the integration density in asynchronous cells.
source: Averaging the integration density at all Sox2 bound sites shows that mitosis integration density is roughly 60% of the integration density in asynchronous cells (Figure 5B, right).
evidence: Supported by ATAC-seq data shown in Figure 5B

claim: The significant decrease in integration density at Sox2 bound regions may reflect the reduced residence time of Sox2 at these sites during mitosis.
source: This significant decrease in integration density at Sox2 bound regions may reflect the reduced residence time of Sox2 at these sites during mitosis (Figure 2D), and is consistent with a previous study showing decreased accessibility at enhancer regions (Hsiung et al., 2015).
evidence: Inferred from ATAC-seq data and single particle tracking data, and consistent with published literature

claim: Footprinting analysis shows nearly identical integration patterns and footprinting depth for asynchronous and mitotic cells at Sox2 motif sites.
source: This footprinting analysis shows nearly identical integration patterns and footprinting depth for asynchronous and mitotic cells that is absent in matching random genomic sites, suggesting that Sox2 can sample binding sites as equally well in mitotic as in asynchronous cells.
evidence: Supported by ATAC-seq footprinting data shown in Figure 5C

claim: Sox2 can sample binding sites as equally well in mitotic as in asynchronous cells.
source: This footprinting analysis shows nearly identical integration patterns and footprinting depth for asynchronous and mitotic cells that is absent in matching random genomic sites, suggesting that Sox2 can sample binding sites as equally well in mitotic as in asynchronous cells.
evidence: Inferred from ATAC-seq footprinting data showing similar patterns in mitotic and asynchronous cells

claim: Sox2 scans its binding sites relatively quickly through its DNA binding domain and is stabilized through the TAD when transcription is activated.
source: This interpretation is consistent with the similar binding dynamics of the Sox2 HMG domain in interphase and in mitosis (Figure 3B), lending further support for the model that Sox2 scans its binding sites relatively quickly through its DNA binding domain and is stabilized through the TAD when transcription is activated.
evidence: Inferred from ATAC-seq footprinting data and FRAP data

claim: Within 10 s after PFA addition, Halo-Sox2 levels at the chromosomes are visibly reduced.
source: Within 10 s after PFA addition, Halo-Sox2 levels at the chromosomes are visibly reduced, and becomes almost indistinguishable from the cytoplasmic signal by 60 s after PFA addition (Figure 6A).
evidence: Supported by time-lapse imaging data shown in Figure 6A

claim: At 60 s post PFA addition, chromosome enrichment of Halo-Sox2 decreased as the concentration of PFA added is increased.
source: At 60 s post PFA addition, chromosome enrichment of Halo-Sox2 decreased as the concentration of PFA added is increased (Figure 6B), confirming that the fixation artifact is dose-dependent.
evidence: Supported by time-lapse imaging data shown in Figure 6B

claim: Halo-TBP is resistant to PFA mis-localization compared to the highly dynamic Halo-NLS.
source: Compared to the highly dynamic Halo-NLS, Halo-TBP is resistant to PFA mis-localization (Figure 6C).
evidence: Supported by imaging data shown in Figure 6C

claim: Active nuclear import had no effect on PFA-induced mis-localization as Halo-Plant NLS also becomes excluded from mitotic chromosomes after fixation.
source: Furthermore, whereas active nuclear import is required for chromosome enrichment, it had no effect on PFA-induced mis-localization as Halo-Plant NLS also becomes excluded from mitotic chromosomes after fixation, in contrast to Halo-only control (Figure 6C).
evidence: Supported by imaging data shown in Figure 6C

claim: High pressure freezing followed by freeze substitution partially rescues the localization of Halo-Sox2 on mitotic chromosomes.
source: Under these conditions, we partially rescued the localization of Halo-Sox2 on mitotic chromosomes, suggesting that the HPF-FS method can somewhat counteract the PFA-induced artifact.
evidence: Supported by imaging data shown in Figure 6D

claim: Highly dynamic TFs are more susceptible to PFA-induced mis-localization.
source: Taken together, these results point to a robust artifact caused by formaldehyde based cross-linking, and support a model whereby highly dynamic TFs are more susceptible to PFA-induced mis-localization.
evidence: Inferred from data showing dose-dependent effects and differential susceptibility based on TF dynamics

claim: During mitosis, transcription is shut off, chromatin condenses, and most transcription factors are reported to be excluded from chromosomes.
source: During mitosis, transcription is shut off, chromatin condenses, and most transcription factors (TFs) are reported to be excluded from chromosomes.
evidence: Represents established knowledge in the field as stated in the abstract

claim: Many TFs remain associated with chromosomes in mouse embryonic stem cells.
source: Here we report instead that many TFs remain associated with chromosomes in mouse embryonic stem cells, and that the exclusion previously described is largely a fixation artifact.
evidence: Supported by live-cell imaging data throughout the manuscript

claim: The exclusion of TFs from mitotic chromosomes previously described is largely a fixation artifact.
source: Here we report instead that many TFs remain associated with chromosomes in mouse embryonic stem cells, and that the exclusion previously described is largely a fixation artifact.
evidence: Supported by comparison of live-cell imaging versus fixed cell imaging data

claim: Most TFs tested are significantly enriched on mitotic chromosomes.
source: In particular, most TFs we tested are significantly enriched on mitotic chromosomes.
evidence: Supported by live-cell imaging data shown in Figure 1I

claim: The mitotic interaction of Sox2 is more dynamic than in interphase.
source: Studies with Sox2 reveal that this mitotic interaction is more dynamic than in interphase and is facilitated by both DNA binding and nuclear import.
evidence: Supported by FRAP and single particle tracking data

claim: The mitotic interaction of Sox2 is facilitated by both DNA binding and nuclear import.
source: Studies with Sox2 reveal that this mitotic interaction is more dynamic than in interphase and is facilitated by both DNA binding and nuclear import.
evidence: Supported by experiments with DNA binding mutants and NLS mutants shown in Figure 2

claim: The dynamic mode of Sox2 interaction with mitotic chromosomes results from lack of transcriptional activation rather than decreased accessibility of underlying DNA sequences in mitosis.
source: Furthermore, this dynamic mode results from lack of transcriptional activation rather than decreased accessibility of underlying DNA sequences in mitosis.
evidence: Inferred from FRAP data showing Sox2 HMG (lacking TAD) behaves similarly in interphase and mitosis, and ATAC-seq data showing maintained accessibility

claim: In mitosis, the global transcriptional machinery is inactivated via a cell cycle-dependent phosphorylation cascade.
source: In mitosis, the global transcriptional machinery is inactivated via a cell cycle-dependent phosphorylation cascade (Prescott and Bender, 1962; Rhind and Russell, 2012; Taylor, 1960).
evidence: Supported by citations to Prescott and Bender, 1962; Rhind and Russell, 2012; Taylor, 1960

claim: Interphase chromatin organizes into highly condensed mitotic chromosomes.
source: Interphase chromatin organizes into highly condensed mitotic chromosomes (Koshland and Strunnikov, 1995), and the nuclear envelope is disassembled (Terasaki et al., 2001).
evidence: Supported by citations to Koshland and Strunnikov, 1995; Terasaki et al., 2001

claim: The nuclear envelope is disassembled during mitosis.
source: Interphase chromatin organizes into highly condensed mitotic chromosomes (Koshland and Strunnikov, 1995), and the nuclear envelope is disassembled (Terasaki et al., 2001).
evidence: Supported by citation to Terasaki et al., 2001

claim: Most transcription factors have been shown to be excluded from mitotic chromosomes.
source: Furthermore, most transcription factors (TFs) have been shown to be excluded from mitotic chromosomes (Gottesfeld and Forbes, 1997; John and Workman, 1998; Martínez-Balbás et al., 1995; Rizkallah and Hurt, 2009), leading to the conclusion that mitotic chromosomes may be inaccessible to DNA binding and exclude most TFs.
evidence: Supported by citations to Gottesfeld and Forbes, 1997; John and Workman, 1998; Martínez-Balbás et al., 1995; Rizkallah and Hurt, 2009

claim: DNase I hypersensitive sites on the human hsp70 locus were shown to be maintained in mitotic chromosomes.
source: For example, DNase I hypersensitive sites on the human hsp70 locus were shown to be maintained in mitotic chromosomes (Martínez-Balbás et al., 1995) implying the presence of a 'bookmarker' to keep the region accessible to nuclease digestion.
evidence: Supported by citation to Martínez-Balbás et al., 1995

claim: The transcription start sites of certain genes scheduled for reactivation following mitosis were shown to remain sensitive to permanganate oxidation in mitosis.
source: Similarly, the transcription start sites (TSSs) of certain genes scheduled for reactivation following mitosis were shown to remain sensitive to permanganate oxidation in mitosis, suggesting a conformationally privileged structure at the TSSs of these genes (Michelotti et al., 1997).
evidence: Supported by citation to Michelotti et al., 1997

claim: HSF2 was shown to bind at the hsp70i locus during mitosis.
source: It was therefore a significant step in resolving this conundrum when HSF2 was shown to bind at the hsp70i locus during mitosis (Xing et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to Xing et al., 2005

claim: GATA1 has previously been reported to be excluded from mitotic chromosomes by immunofluorescence.
source: For instance, GATA1, a major regulator of the erythroid lineage, has previously been reported to be excluded from mitotic chromosomes by immunofluorescence (Xin et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to Xin et al., 2007

claim: GATA1 actually remained bound on its target regions during mitosis as shown by live-cell imaging and chromatin immunoprecipitation analysis.
source: Subsequently, the Blobel group has shown, by live-cell imaging and chromatin immunoprecipitation analysis, that GATA1 actually remained bound on its target regions during mitosis (Kadauke et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kadauke et al., 2012

claim: TFs such as GATA1 act as the elusive 'bookmark' that maintain chromatin architecture at regulatory regions.
source: TFs such as GATA1 seem to act as the elusive 'bookmark' that maintain chromatin architecture at regulatory regions, and thus have been termed mitotic bookmarkers.
evidence: Inferred from the finding that GATA1 remains bound during mitosis

claim: The synchronization strategy achieves about 95% pure mitotic population.
source: We synchronized cells at various stages of the cell cycle and obtained about 95% pure mitotic population. (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry and immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1

claim: All of Sox2-detected molecules for each Halo-Sox2 KI clone are migrating higher than the wild-type Sox2 suggesting that all molecules contain the HaloTag.
source: All of Sox2-detected molecules for each clone are migrating higher than the wild-type Sox2 suggesting that all molecules contain the HaloTag.
evidence: Supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3A

claim: Halo-Sox2 KI cells maintain pluripotency.
source: We obtained three independent clones that were homozygously tagged (Halo-Sox2 KI), and confirmed that the tagging has no detectable effect on Sox2 function as Halo-Sox2 KI ES cells maintain pluripotency (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by teratoma assay data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3C

claim: TFs of the RNA Polymerase I machinery have been shown to rapidly exchange on and off ribosomal DNA clusters during mitosis through FRAP analysis.
source: For example, TFs of the RNA Polymerase I machinery have been shown to rapidly exchange on and off ribosomal DNA clusters during mitosis through FRAP analysis (Chen et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to Chen et al., 2005

claim: Diffusion of EGFP molecules is delayed but not hindered through mitotic chromosomes as measured by pair correlation function.
source: Diffusion of EGFP molecules is delayed but not hindered through mitotic chromosomes as measured by pair correlation function, suggesting that molecules can freely cross chromosomes during mitosis (Hinde et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Hinde et al., 2011

claim: Although there is a global decrease in DNase-seq signals during mitosis, overall patterns of DNase I HS patterns are preserved.
source: More recently, the Blobel group has performed DNase I hypersensitivity assay coupled with sequencing in mitotic and asynchronous mouse erythroblast cells and has shown that, although there is a global decrease in DNase-seq signals during mitosis, overall patterns of DNase I HS patterns are preserved (Hsiung et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Hsiung et al., 2015

claim: DNA in mitotic chromosomes is as accessible as in interphase chromatin.
source: Taken together, these studies suggest that DNA in mitotic chromosomes is as accessible as in interphase chromatin.
evidence: Inferred from multiple studies including ATAC-seq data and published literature

claim: At any given time during interphase, roughly 70% of Sox2 molecules are undergoing diffusion while 30% are bound.
source: Our fast-tracking SPT experiments have revealed that, at any given time during interphase, roughly 70% of Sox2 molecules are undergoing diffusion while 30% are bound.
evidence: Supported by single particle tracking data shown in Figure 3E

claim: The interphase long-lived stable binding events of Sox2 are highly dependent on the TAD-mediated protein-protein interactions that occur during transcriptional activation.
source: Here, we have confirmed that the interphase long-lived stable binding events are highly dependent on the TAD-mediated protein-protein interactions that occur during transcriptional activation (Chen et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by FRAP data and citation to Chen et al., 2014

claim: During mitosis, an average of 82% of Sox2 molecules are freely diffusing.
source: During mitosis when the nuclear envelope is disassembled and DNA becomes highly condensed, we have observed an increase in the fraction of freely diffusing Sox2 molecules to an average of 82%.
evidence: Inferred from single particle tracking data showing 18.3% bound in mitosis

claim: The 18% of Sox2 molecules that are bound on mitotic chromosomes exhibit decreased residence times relative to bound Sox2 molecules in interphase.
source: Interestingly, the 18% of Sox2 molecules that are bound on mitotic chromosomes exhibit decreased residence times relative to bound Sox2 molecules in interphase.
evidence: Supported by single particle tracking data shown in Figure 3D

claim: Sox2 dynamics in mitosis mimics the behavior of interphase Sox2 without its transcriptional activation domain.
source: Indeed, Sox2 dynamics in mitosis mimics the behavior of interphase Sox2 without its transcriptional activation domain, suggesting that Sox2 protein-protein interactions dependent on transcriptional activation are severely abrogated in mitosis.
evidence: Supported by FRAP data showing similar recovery times for Sox2 HMG in interphase and full-length Sox2 in mitosis

claim: Sox2 behavior during mitosis appears to be dominated by two main factors, 3D diffusion and protein-DNA contacts.
source: Therefore, in contrast to interphase cells, Sox2 behavior during mitosis appears to be dominated by two main factors, 3D diffusion and protein-DNA contacts.
evidence: Inferred from FRAP and single particle tracking data showing loss of TAD-mediated stabilization in mitosis

claim: FoxA1 has been shown to bind to mitotic chromosomes in a more dynamic manner than to interphase chromatin.
source: Similarly, FoxA1, another TF that has been described as a mitotic bookmarker, has also been shown to bind to mitotic chromosomes in a more dynamic manner than to interphase chromatin (Caravaca et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Caravaca et al., 2013

claim: RCC1 remains localized at mitotic chromosomes, thereby maintaining the Ran-GTP gradient in mitosis.
source: Despite nuclear envelope breakdown during mitosis, RCC1 remains localized at mitotic chromosomes, thereby maintaining the Ran-GTP gradient in mitosis (Moore et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citation to Moore et al., 2002

claim: The Ran-GTP gradient has been shown to be vital in accurate formation of the spindle assembly during mitosis through the re-purposing of the canonical import proteins.
source: This Ran-GTP gradient has recently been shown to be vital in accurate formation of the spindle assembly during mitosis through the re-purposing of the canonical import proteins (Forbes et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Forbes et al., 2015

claim: The accumulation of NLS containing proteins on chromosomes was hypothesized and modeled previously.
source: Indeed, the accumulation of NLS containing proteins on chromosomes was hypothesized and modeled previously (Caudron et al., 2005) and a drug-dependent block of nuclear import resulted in exclusion of a TF mutant from mitotic chromosomes (Lerner et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Caudron et al., 2005 and Lerner et al., 2016

claim: A drug-dependent block of nuclear import resulted in exclusion of a TF mutant from mitotic chromosomes.
source: Indeed, the accumulation of NLS containing proteins on chromosomes was hypothesized and modeled previously (Caudron et al., 2005) and a drug-dependent block of nuclear import resulted in exclusion of a TF mutant from mitotic chromosomes (Lerner et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lerner et al., 2016

claim: Active shuttling of nuclear proteins to the chromosomes would facilitate the accumulation of high local concentrations of nuclear factors near the chromosomes to ensure an efficient re-establishment of the nuclear environment immediately following mitosis when the nuclear envelope reforms.
source: This postulated active shuttling of nuclear proteins to the chromosomes serves two potential functions. First, such a mechanism would facilitate the accumulation of high local concentrations of nuclear factors near the chromosomes to ensure an efficient re-establishment of the nuclear environment immediately following mitosis when the nuclear envelope reforms.
evidence: Speculative reasoning based on the maintained Ran-GTP gradient and nuclear import machinery during mitosis

claim: The increased local concentration of TFs on mitotic chromosomes may contribute to maintaining the accessibility of DNA regulatory regions by facilitating increased TF-chromosome interactions.
source: Secondly, the increased local concentration of TFs on mitotic chromosomes may contribute to maintaining the accessibility of DNA regulatory regions, the original definition of mitotic bookmarking, even under the highly condensed state of mitotic chromosomes by facilitating increased TF-chromosome interactions.
evidence: Speculative reasoning based on the observed enrichment of TFs on mitotic chromosomes and maintained DNA accessibility

claim: Most TFs can and do interact with mitotic chromosomes and thus function as general mitotic bookmarkers.
source: Therefore, most TFs can and do interact with mitotic chromosomes and thus function as general mitotic bookmarkers.
evidence: Inferred from live-cell imaging data showing most TFs associate with mitotic chromosomes and ATAC-seq data showing maintained accessibility

claim: Factors such as CTCF, the cohesin complex, and DNA topoisomerases exhibit stable binding and have been shown by fixed immunofluorescence to remain bound on mitotic chromosomes.
source: Indeed, some indications of this latter point exist in the literature. For example, factors such as CTCF, the cohesin complex, and DNA topoisomerases, all of which exhibit stable binding, have been shown by fixed immunofluorescence to remain bound on mitotic chromosomes (Burke et al., 2005; Christensen et al., 2002; Losada and Hirano, 2001; Nakahashi et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Burke et al., 2005; Christensen et al., 2002; Losada and Hirano, 2001; Nakahashi et al., 2013

claim: ChIP studies reliant on formaldehyde cross-linking may underestimate the total binding space of any given TF.
source: Chromatin immunoprecipitation (ChIP) studies reliant on formaldehyde cross-linking may underestimate the total binding space of any given TF.
evidence: Inferred from the finding that formaldehyde fixation causes TF exclusion from mitotic chromosomes

claim: Studies designed to measure the dynamics of TFs through time-course cross-linked chromatin immunoprecipitation experiments may be susceptible to formaldehyde-based artifacts.
source: Furthermore, studies designed to measure the dynamics of TFs through time-course cross-linked chromatin immunoprecipitation experiments (Lickwar et al., 2012) may be susceptible to formaldehyde-based artifacts.
evidence: Inferred from the finding that formaldehyde fixation causes TF exclusion and speculative reasoning about implications for ChIP experiments

claim: Previous examples of limitations in ChIP due to formaldehyde have been documented.
source: Indeed, previous examples of this limitation in ChIP have been documented (Schmiedeberg et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Schmiedeberg et al., 2009

claim: Formaldehyde molecules rapidly cross-link to the nearest protein as they cross the cell membrane, resulting in a cross-linking gradient that moves from the cell membrane inward.
source: Formaldehyde molecules rapidly cross-link to the nearest protein as they cross the cell membrane, resulting in a cross-linking gradient that moves from the cell membrane inward.
evidence: Proposed mechanistic model based on chemical properties of formaldehyde and observed effects

claim: The advancing gradient of cross-linking would result in depletion of cytoplasmic TF molecules as they are cross-linked first, reducing the effective kon rates.
source: The advancing gradient of cross-linking would result in depletion of cytoplasmic TF molecules as they are cross-linked first, reducing the effective kon rates.
evidence: Proposed mechanistic model based on the cross-linking gradient hypothesis

claim: Most TFs have a residence time of under 20 s and are thus quite dynamic even during interphase.
source: We note that recent studies have shown, using live-cell single molecule tracking and FRAP experiments, that most TFs have a residence time of under 20 s and are thus quite dynamic even during interphase (Chen et al., 2014; Elf et al., 2007; Gebhardt et al., 2013; Mueller et al., 2008; Swinstead et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Chen et al., 2014; Elf et al., 2007; Gebhardt et al., 2013; Mueller et al., 2008; Swinstead et al., 2016
